title: Instructions on Investigating Buddha-Recitation
author: Annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: From the Dream-Wandering Collection: A Reply to the Monk Haiyin of Huzhou

inline.s: Dream-Wandering Collection
: A Reply to the Monk Haiyin of Huzhou)
By investigation one blocks the faculty of intellect, so that delusive thoughts no longer arise.
A hundred years, thirty-six thousand mornings; turn it over and over — it was always this fellow.

[Question: In Chan meditation, what matters is that not a single thought arises; in Buddha-recitation, what matters is that pure thoughts continue without interruption. This practice of investigating Buddha-recitation aims at wondrous awakening and the attainment of rebirth in the Pure Land. Now, when reciting the Buddha's name, mind and Buddha are clearly distinct; but when investigating, both are cut off at once. Thus the work of investigation gradually prevails while the recitation gradually fades. How then, at the end, can one both awaken and attain rebirth?]

Question: In Chan meditation, what matters is that not a single thought arises; in Buddha-recitation, what matters is that pure thoughts continue without interruption. This practice of investigating Buddha-recitation aims at wondrous awakening and the attainment of rebirth in the Pure Land. Now when one recites the Buddha's name, the mind that recites and the Buddha that is recited are perfectly distinct; but when one investigates, what matters is that not a single thought arises, so that there is neither a reciting mind nor a recited Buddha (both are cut off at once). Thus the work of investigation gradually prevails and the work of recitation gradually fades. How, then, at the moment of death, can one both awaken and attain rebirth?

[How then, at the end, can one both awaken and attain rebirth?] How can one, at the moment of death, both awaken and attain rebirth? The questioner is worried: if the investigation of Buddha-recitation reaches the point where not a single thought arises, then, since no Buddha's name remains in the mind, can one still attain rebirth? In the answer that follows, Master Hanshan teaches: the Buddha's name continuing without interruption is called continuous mindfulness, not continuous pure thought. Only when not a single thought arises can pure thoughts truly continue. Having reached this state of uninterrupted pure thought, one not only attains rebirth but attains the highest grade of the highest class.

[Answer: It is indeed so that in Chan meditation what matters is that not a single thought arises. But as for Buddha-recitation, when you say that what matters is that pure thoughts continue without interruption, that is merely taking the four-syllable Buddha's name and placing it in the mind as a pure thought. You do not realize that the four-syllable Buddha's name continuing without interruption is called continuous mindfulness, not continuous pure thought. It belongs to people of middling and lesser faculties, who devote themselves to Buddha-recitation in quest of rebirth in the West: it is precisely the expedient gateway of the Pure Land.]
Answer:
When you say '
in Chan meditation what matters is that no single thought arises
that
is correct
But when you say '
in Buddha-recitation what matters is that pure thoughts continue without interruption
that means

you take the four-syllable Buddha's name and place it in your mind as a pure thought. You do not realize that when the four-syllable Buddha's name continues unbroken (not interrupted by delusive thoughts), this is called continuous mindfulness,
not
continuous pure thought. It is for people of middling and lesser faculties, who devote themselves to Buddha-recitation in quest of rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss; this
is

[Now, when it is said that the investigation of Buddha-recitation aims at wondrous awakening, this means taking a single sound of the Buddha's name as a huatou to investigate — what is called the koan of reciting the Buddha's name and investigating Chan. It is just as the patriarchs of old taught people to investigate huatou, such as 'the cypress tree in the courtyard,' 'three pounds of flax,' 'a dried lump of dung,' 'a dog has no Buddha-nature,' 'put it down,' 'Mount Sumeru,' and other koans. Take up any one of these and keep it in your breast, silently investigating it, and by this means block the faculty of intellect so that delusive thoughts no longer arise. In time, when the huatou gains power, suddenly there comes a great crash, like a bean bursting in cold ashes, and the nest of ignorance and karmic consciousness is crushed to pieces at a single press. This is wondrous awakening.]

When it is said that 'the practice of investigating Buddha-recitation aims at wondrous awakening,' this means taking a single sound of the Buddha's name as a huatou to investigate — what is called the koan of reciting the Buddha's name and investigating Chan. It is just as the patriarchs of old taught people to investigate huatou, such as 'the cypress tree in the courtyard,' 'three pounds of flax,' 'a dried lump of dung,' 'a dog has no Buddha-nature,' 'put it down,' 'Mount Sumeru,' and other koans. Take up any one of these huatou and keep it in your breast, silently investigating it,
and by this means block the faculty of intellect so that delusive thoughts no longer arise

. In time, when the huatou gains power, suddenly there comes a great crash, like a bean bursting in cold ashes, and the nest of ignorance and karmic consciousness is crushed to pieces at a single press. This is wondrous awakening.
[Nest and burrow (ke jiu): a ready-made mold, an old rut. Press (za): to squeeze, to crush.]
[The investigation of Buddha-recitation is practiced in the same way: simply raise a single sound of the Buddha's name, and then doubt and examine — who is it that recites? Look deeply into
(qu)

it and investigate: from where does this Buddha arise? Who, after all, is the one who recites? Doubt on and on in this way, investigate again and again, and in time, when it gains power, you will suddenly awaken. This is the koan of verifying Buddha-recitation, and it is no different from investigating a huatou. In the end one must investigate to the point where not a single thought arises: this is pure thought.]
And
the investigation of Buddha-recitation
is practiced
in the same way: simply raise a single sound of the Buddha's
name
and then doubt and examine
: who is it that recites
the Buddha?
Peer deeply and investigate
(to doubt and examine is to peer and investigate,
not to use the conscious mind to ponder and conjecture
); from where does this
Buddha's name
arise, and who, after all, is the one who recites
the Buddha

? Doubt on and on in this way, investigate again and again, and in time, when it gains power, you will suddenly awaken (suddenly there comes a great crash, like a bean bursting in cold ashes, and the nest of ignorance and karmic consciousness is crushed to pieces at a single press). This is the koan of verifying Buddha-recitation, and it is no different from investigating a huatou (
both use it to block the faculty of intellect so that delusive thoughts no longer arise
). In the end one must investigate to the point where not a single thought arises;
only this is
pure thought.

[The Great Calming and Contemplation says: 'If the mind scatters, gather it in and return it to right mindfulness.' Right mindfulness is no-thought. Only no-thought is pure thought; it is simply that right mindfulness remains undimmed, and this is what continuity means. How could the unbroken sound of the Buddha's name, voice after voice, be taken as the pure thought of investigation? Such a one knows neither Chan nor Buddha-recitation. If investigation truly brings pure thought to the fore, then the Pure Land need not be sought outside, for a single thought arrives there — attaining the highest grade of the highest class is the natural outcome of such practice.]

Right mindfulness is no-thought. No-thought
alone
is pure thought

[One who does not know Buddha-recitation either] Mr. Jiang Weinong says in his Lectures on the Diamond Sutra:
"Know that the aim of Buddha-recitation must be to return to no-thought, which is to return to suchness
(the true nature)
, so that without speaking of cutting off, thoughts are cut off of themselves
(without speaking of cutting off thoughts, the thoughts are cut off of themselves)
, and without aiming at realization, one realizes of itself
(to realize: to see the true nature completely)
, so how great is its expediency!"
(See
Reciting Without Reciting
for details.)

[Attaining the highest grade of the highest class] This answers the question 'How then, at the end, can one both awaken and attain rebirth?' The questioner is worried that if the investigation of Buddha-recitation reaches the point where not a single thought arises, then, since no Buddha's name remains in the mind, can one still attain rebirth? Master Hanshan replies: when not a single thought arises, that alone is pure thoughts continuing without interruption. Having reached this state (
"pure thought brought to the fore"
) one not only attains rebirth, but attains the highest grade of the highest class.
Master Hanshan said:
"Though koans are many, the huatou of verifying Buddha-recitation
(that is, investigating 'Who recites the Buddha's name?')
is the easiest to gain power with amid the dust of afflictions."
(Dream-Wandering Collection
A Reply to Vice Censor-in-Chief Zheng Kunyan)
Master Hanshan said:

"In the koan of verifying Buddha-recitation, one simply raises a single sound of Amitābha Buddha as the huatou, and at the very point of raising it brings forth doubt: one asks who it is that recites the Buddha's name. Raise it again and examine again, examine and examine once more: see
(that is,

who, after all, is the one reciting the Buddha's name). Settle steadily on the huatou in this way, and all delusive and scattered thoughts are cut off at once, like cutting through tangled silk; they are no longer allowed to arise, and wherever they arise they vanish. Only one thought remains, vividly and solitarily clear, like the white sun in an empty sky. Delusive thoughts do not arise, confusion recedes of itself: utterly still, yet keenly aware."
(Dream-Wandering Collection
Essential Points on Buddha-Recitation and Chan Investigation)
[At the very point of raising it, bring forth doubt, and ask who it is that recites the Buddha's name] The concrete practice is this: peer deeply and investigate. Master Hanshan said:
"The investigation of Buddha-recitation is practiced in the same way: simply raise a single sound of the Buddha's name, and then doubt and examine — who is it?
Peer deeply and investigate
; from where does this Buddha
(this Buddha's name)

arise, and who, after all, is the one who recites? Doubt on and on in this way, investigate again and again, and in time, when it gains power, you will suddenly awaken. This is the koan of verifying Buddha-recitation, and it is no different from investigating a huatou. In the end one must investigate to the point where not a single thought arises: this is pure thought."
(Dream-Wandering Collection
A Reply to the Monk Haiyin of Huzhou)
[Utterly still, yet keenly aware]
It means: no-thought, and yet not losing clear awareness.
Utterly still
means not a single thought arises
; keenly aware means the mind is clear and alert, not losing clear awareness. Master Yongjia said:
Still and aware — this is right; still and blank — this is wrong. Aware and still — this is right; aware and scattered — this is wrong.
" [Avyākṛta (wuji), the undetermined] here means dullness, the loss of clear awareness.
Master Hanshan said:

"How is it that investigation is itself Buddha-recitation, and Buddha-recitation is itself investigation? In investigating today, simply take the phrase 'Amitābha' as your huatou and do the work of verification. Put down all at once your own body, mind, and world, together with all your former worldly notions, habitual turns of speech, and Buddhist views and opinions. Then, from within emptiness and stillness, raise up with effort a single sound of Amitābha Buddha, perfectly clear and distinct. Just as you raise it, look directly into it and verify who it is that recites the Buddha's name. Bring forth doubt once more
(the doubt spoken of here means gathering your whole mind to look into and investigate: who is it that recites the Buddha's name?)
, and examine and examine again
(the examination spoken of here means looking into and investigating)
, doubting and doubting again, like a donkey gazing into a well."

[Like a donkey gazing into a well] This illustrates investigating beyond the discriminations of feeling and consciousness. The Record of Caoshan says: "The Master (Chan Master Caoshan Benji Yuanzheng) asked Elder De: 'The Buddha's true dharma-body is like empty space; it manifests forms in response to things, like the moon in water. How would you express the principle of this response (how is this principle to be put into words)?' De said: 'Like a donkey gazing into a well.' Caoshan said: 'You have only said eighty percent of it.' De said: 'How would you say it, Master (what would you say, Reverend)?' Caoshan said: 'Like a well gazing at the donkey.'"

Gaze on and on, doubt on and on, until doubt reaches the point where the paths of mind and thought are cut off, like a mountain of silver or a wall of iron, with no place to turn or breathe. Then suddenly you bump into it, touch it; truly there is no room for birth-and-death, and suddenly it appears before you with a rush. At that moment the whole body streams with sweat, as if waking from a great dream. Only then do you believe that birth is no-birth and no-birth is birth; that investigation is recitation and recitation is investigation. Looking back, you realize that all along you were like one searching for Chang'an while standing inside the Hanyuan Hall.

[Like searching for Chang'an inside the Hanyuan Hall] The Hanyuan Hall was the principal hall of the imperial palace in Chang'an, the Tang dynasty capital. 'Searching for Chang'an inside the Hanyuan Hall' illustrates seeking to become a Buddha when one is a Buddha already.

"In doing this work, the greatest danger is wanting to awaken. As soon as the mind wants to awaken, that is a board blocking your view. Just keep at it without reckoning the stages. And when you reach the point where you can no longer go on, then rouse your spirits
(rouse your energy)

, and begin all over again. Furthermore, never crave the marvelous. Even if a thought momentarily subsides and you feel still and joyful, do not take this as something good; you must spit it out. Never take the profound sayings and wondrous words of the Buddhas and patriarchs as proof and treat them as the Dharma, and never fall into the armor of doing-nothing and consider that attainment. In short, pay no heed to saint or ordinary being, to delusion or awakening; single-mindedly seek where a single thought comes to rest. Pursue it to the point where it is utterly driven out, and in time you will see your original face for yourself, like seeing your own father at the crossroads — no need to ask anyone. Seen in this way, this matter is from the outset everyone's own business, with nothing especially extraordinary about it. If a practitioner, truly and honestly, for the sake of the great matter of birth and death, tries setting to work here, he will certainly not be cheated."
(Dream-Wandering Collection: Instructions to Shen Dajie)

[The head-blocking board] A board that blocks one's line of sight; it illustrates how the mind that wants to awaken is itself an obstacle veiling the path. [The armor of doing-nothing] A shell of having nothing to do, meaning sitting in empty quiescence with neither delusive thoughts nor investigation. Chan Master Fayen said: "You must rouse your energies sharply, take up a huatou, and investigate it day and night, grappling with it. Do not sit inside the armor of doing-nothing, and do not sit rigidly on the cushion. If scattered thoughts multiply the more you struggle with them, set them down lightly, get up and walk about, then return to the cushion. Open both eyes, clench both fists, straighten your spine, and raise the huatou as before. You will then feel cool and clear, like a pot of boiling soup into which a ladle of cold water has been poured. Working in this way, the time of arrival is certain." (Outline of the Buddha-Patriarchs) [Like seeing your own father at the crossroads] Like seeing your own father at the crossroads and recognizing him at a glance. It illustrates knowing with certainty that this is the original face, without error.
Master Hanshan said:
"Simply put down all at once the delusive thoughts of the past
(put down all at once the delusive thoughts you have been spinning right now)

, and do not let them secretly arise. Slowly and single-mindedly raise a single sound of Amitābha Buddha, settle firmly upon it, and observe where this thought arises, like casting a fishing line into a deep pool. If delusive thoughts arise again, this is because beginningless habit is too heavy; put them down again
(again put down all at once the delusive thoughts you are spinning right now)

. Never use the mind to cut off delusive thoughts; simply straighten your spine, do not think east or west, and steadily observe the very place where delusive thoughts arise. Put down and put down again
(put down, and put down again, the delusive thoughts you are spinning right now)
, then slowly raise another sound of the Buddha, and steadily observe this one sound of the Buddha
(the Buddha's name)

— from where, after all, does it arise? By the fifth or seventh repetition delusive thoughts no longer arise. Then bring forth doubt again and examine who, in the end, is reciting the Buddha's name. People of the world take this as a mere phrase to be spoken
(people of the world take 'Who recites the Buddha's name?' as a mere phrase to be spoken)

, not realizing that bringing forth doubt in this way is precisely where the power lies. If delusive thoughts arise again, simply cry 'Ho!' and ask only 'Who?' — the delusive thought is swept away and vanishes on the spot. The Buddha said: 'Except when asleep, always gather the mind.' While asleep one cannot gather the mind; as soon as one wakes, raise the huatou. Not only in sitting is it so; in walking, standing, eating, drinking, moving and resting it is the same. In a dense crowd, one does not see that anyone is there; amid many movements, one does not see any movement. In this way one gradually finds an entry, and the seventh consciousness
(manas)
no longer functions here."
(Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions to the Chan Adept Yujue)
Master Hanshan said:

"When the ancients taught people to investigate Chan and do the work, they first required that inwardly one be free of body and mind and outwardly let go of the world, putting everything down without a trace remaining. Then one simply raises a single koan huatou, such as 'Zhaozhou: Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? Zhou said: No,' or 'The ten thousand dharmas return to the One; where does the One return to?' or the verification 'Who recites the Buddha's name?' Take up any one and lay it across your breast like a diamond king's sword, cutting off all thoughts and delusive imaginings at once, like cutting through tangled silk. Inside, nothing is allowed out; outside, nothing is allowed in; block the vital pass, seal the throat, allow no breath to escape. Strive in this way, and with a single glance look into it: what, after all, is this thing that raises the huatou? Doubt in this way. Doubt on and on until your mind is like a wall, no longer permitting a second thought to arise. As soon as a delusive thought secretly trickles forth, catch sight of it with one glance, then raise the huatou with all your might and bring forth doubt again. Examine and doubt, and press this mass of doubt until it is stopped up. When thoughts no longer arise and delusive thinking no longer functions, this is precisely where the power lies. Settle firmly in this way through all walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, through movement and stillness, leisure and busyness; clench your teeth and never let go, even in dreams never let go. There is only the one thought of the huatou, which is this person's very life-root, like a dead man who still breathes. Only by laying on such a ruthless hand and grappling this way is one a person who truly works at Chan investigation. When the effort reaches its utmost, without reckoning days or months, suddenly the cold ashes burst with a bean, and that is the season of great joy. But if you drift along carelessly, one day of effort to ten of idleness, I fear you will never find the time of power."
(Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions to the Mountain Master Songpu En)
Master Hanshan said:
"Raise a single sound of the Buddha with effort, and then look at this
(this)

one sound of the Buddha — where does it come from, and where does it now go? Hold steady the diamond eye and fix it with a single gaze. Gaze until there is nowhere to land, then raise again and gaze again, pursuing it until you reach the place where a single thought is unborn, and you will see your original face. At first you use the mind to gaze and pursue; when you have pursued it to the point where both ends of the single thought are cut off, the middle
(the in-between)

stands alone; then from this solitary place swiftly rouse your energies and pursue straight on, and suddenly the mass of doubt bursts apart and your original face appears of itself. This very moment is the true meaning of a single thought's unborn state."
(Dream-Wandering Collection
A Reply to Lord Yuan Cangru)
Master Hanshan said:

"When you look to the point where not a single thought arises, the past and future are cut off and the middle stands alone. Suddenly you smash the lacquer bucket and at once see your original face; body, mind, and world sink away
(vanish)

on the spot, like a flower in the sky dropping its shadow. The ten directions are bright and clear, becoming one great treasury of light. Only then is it the season of arrival; in daily use it stands before you, luminous and perfectly clear, with nothing more to doubt, and you begin to believe that your own mind was like this from the very beginning."
(Dream-Wandering Collection
Essential Points on Buddha-Recitation and Chan Investigation)
Master Hanshan said:
"I dwelt there alone
(when the Master was thirty, at Mount Wutai)
, holding to a single thought. When people came I did not speak, only looked at them. In time I looked on people as I would a stump
wu,
a tree stump)
, until I reached the point of not recognizing a single word.

There was a single-plank bridge over the stream, and day after day I sat or stood upon it. At first the sound of the water was distinct; after a long while, it was heard only when a thought stirred, and not heard when none stirred. One day, sitting on the bridge, I suddenly forgot my body, and the sound fell silent; from then on all sounds were still and troubled me no more.

One day, after the morning gruel, as I was walking in meditation, I suddenly came to a halt: body and mind were gone, and there was only one great treasury of light, perfect, still, and serene, like a great perfect mirror, in which the mountains, rivers, and great earth appeared as reflections. When I came to, I was lucid; I sought body and mind and could not find them at all. Then I spoke a verse: 'The mad mind stills in one sudden flash of thought; / within, without, all faculties and objects clear. / I turn and shatter the vastness of empty space; / the myriad teeming forms arise and vanish here.' From then on, within and without were utterly still, and sounds, forms, and appearances no longer obstructed me; all my former doubts and understandings dissolved on the spot."
(Dream-Wandering Collection: A Veritable Record of the Self-Written Chronological Biography)
Master Hanshan said:
"In my twentieth year,

in the tenth month of that winter, Master Yungu held a Chan retreat at Tianjie Monastery, gathering fifty-three renowned and virtuous ones from within the seas, and opened the gate of sitting meditation. The Master urged me with all his might to go and join. At that time the junior master, the elder
(the monastery abbot)
approved, and so I was able to take part. At first I did not know the secret of applying the mind and suffered greatly. So I offered incense and asked for instruction, and the Master taught me
the koan of verifying Buddha-recitation
(that is, the investigation of Buddha-recitation)
. From then on I investigated it with a single thought that never shifted. For three months I was as if in a dream, never aware that there was an assembly, nor aware of the day's affairs."
(Dream-Wandering Collection: A Veritable Record of the Self-Written Chronological Biography)
From this we can know that both Master Hanshan and Master Lianchi devoted themselves exclusively to the investigation of Buddha-recitation and thereby attained realization.
[Master Lianchi devoted himself exclusively to the investigation of Buddha-recitation]
The Stupa Inscription of Master Lianchi says:
"At first, when the Master set out on his pilgrimage to seek teachers,
he gained power from the investigation of Buddha-recitation
, and thereafter he opened the one gate of the Pure Land, universally gathering the three faculties, and urged it with all his might."
(Translation: At first, when Master Lianchi journeyed on foot to pay respects to good teachers in every quarter,
he gained power from the investigation of Buddha-recitation
, and at that time he opened the one gate of the Pure Land to gather universally the three faculties of superior, middling, and lesser capacity, and urged it with all his might.) It also says:
(Master Lianchi)
At the approach of death, half a month beforehand, he entered the city to take leave of his disciples and old friends."
This shows that Master Lianchi knew the time of his coming beforehand at least half a month in advance.
[Master Hanshan devoted himself exclusively to the investigation of Buddha-recitation] According to
the Dream-Wandering Collection
Self-Written Chronological Biography, it is recorded that
at the age of thirty-three, Master Hanshan wrote out the Avatamsaka Sutra in blood and gold (pricking his tongue for blood and mixing it with gold powder).
No matter whether the strokes were large or small, with every stroke of the brush he recited the Buddha's name once

. Monks and laypeople visiting Mount Wutai came to Miaode Hermitage and invariably asked to see the Master and request Buddhist instruction. Though the Master's hand never stopped copying, he nonetheless did not fail in his responses. Everyone who came to ask was given a few words. As for eminent men and old friends, the Master respectfully invited them to sit on the meditation bed and discussed the Dharma with them, all without hindering the copying in his hand. Day after day he wrote in this way, and though people came and went, in his mind not the least trace of movement was to be found. When the older literary worthies of the neighborhood heard of this, they were astonished and could scarcely believe it. One day the elders brought many of their disciples to the Master's quiet room to verify just what was going on. They deliberately used every means to disturb him, and when he finished a section they compared it with the original; it was indeed without the slightest error, and only then were they convinced that the Master's attainment was extraordinary. But they were greatly puzzled and went to ask Master Miaofeng: 'Why is Master Hanshan able to use his mind for many things at once?' Master Miaofeng replied:
My dharma-brother has long since become thoroughly adept in the samādhi of Buddha-recitation!
Original text
In the sixth year
(the sixth year of Wanli)
, the wuyin year,
I was thirty-three. With single-minded purpose
(with undivided attention)
I copied the sutra.
No matter whether the strokes were large or small, with every stroke I recited the Buddha's name once

. Monks and laypeople visiting the mountain who arrived were invariably announced by an attendant. Though my hand did not stop copying, I did not fail in my responses. Everyone who came to pay respects was given a few words of conversation. Eminent men and old friends I would invite to sit on the meditation bed, and conversing with them I did not fail, nor did it hinder the copying. Comparing it with the original as I wrote, there was not the slightest omission or error. Each day was as usual, without the least trace of movement or stillness. The elders of the neighborhood privately thought this strange and brought several groups to test me, deliberately creating disturbances. When the copying was finished they read it and were fully convinced. So they asked Master Miao: 'How is it that Master Yin can do this?' Master Miao said:
My friend has entered this samādhi
(the samādhi of Buddha-recitation)
and become thoroughly adept
Dream-Wandering Collection
Self-Written Chronological Biography
Master Hanshan says in the Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions to the Chan Adept Xingchu Yuan on Copying Sutras:
This old man
(Hanshan's self-reference)
formerly dwelt at Mount Wutai, where I wrote out the great Avatamsaka Sutra in blood and gold. In the midst of that copying,
regardless of the strokes of the characters, their size or length, with every stroke of the brush I recited the Buddha's name once

. In this way, dot after dot, stroke after stroke, the light of the mind streamed forth; thought after thought unbroken and unforgotten, without error or omission. After a long time it no longer mattered whether I was copying or not, and even in dreams it all became one piece. Thus amid all circumstances, however tumultuous and noisy, the mind remained serene,
attaining the gate of liberation in which one is free and unobstructed amid all circumstances
, so that all that was seen and heard was nothing but the true sutra appearing before me."
In a letter from his later years, Master Hanshan wrote:
Here in my retreat
(within my closed retreat)
I have put all Chan talk and Buddhist teaching up on a high shelf and single-mindedly keep to simple practice
(reciting the Buddha's name with one simple intent; keeping to simple practice here means no longer investigating Chan or studying the teachings)
. I often recall that the ancients recited Amitābha's name a hundred thousand times day and night; now I am ashamed that, being old
(the Master was then seventy-four)
and lacking in physical strength, when I test myself I can usually manage barely half
(more than half, that is, upward of fifty thousand recitations)
. I have specially followed Master Yuan
(Master Huiyuan)
in the six-period lotus clepsydra
(the lotus clepsydra means the lotus water-clock; Huiyao, a disciple of Huiyuan, the first patriarch of the Pure Land school, used a lotus flower as a time-measuring device at the Lushan monastery)
, using incense instead of the flower
(I burn incense to mark the time in place of the lotus clepsydra)
. For several months now,
body and mind have of themselves reached ultimate bliss
(Dream-Wandering Collection
A Reply to the Grand Scribe Qian Shouzhi)
The Master's Chronological Biography records:
(Wanli)
In the forty-seventh year, the jiwei year, I was seventy-four. ... On the full moon of the eighth month
(the fifteenth day of the eighth month)
, I entered retreat and put aside affairs, following Master Yuan in marking the six periods with incense instead of the clepsydra,
devoting myself single-mindedly to the Pure Land practice
Master Hanshan passed into nirvāṇa on the thirteenth day of the tenth month of the third year of Tianqi (
), at the age of seventy-eight. According to the Annotated Chronological Biography of Master Hanshan:
"At midday
the thirteenth day of the tenth month
, noon)
, Lord Zhang
(Zhang Sanxing, prefect of Shaoyang, who had come into the mountains to present a purple silk Chan robe in celebration of the Master's birthday;
the twelfth day of the tenth month
was the Master's birthday)

took his leave. The Master at once called an attendant to fetch pure water to rinse his mouth, and said: 'Today I cut off the tangled vines.' He then called for hot water, bathed, and changed his robes, while
the assembled crowd surrounded him reciting the Buddha's name
. He instructed them: 'Do not be alarmed. Follow the Buddha's rule: do not wear hempen mourning, do not weep,
single-mindedly recite the Buddha's name
.' At the hour of shen
(three in the afternoon)

, the Master sat upright and passed away. That night a brilliant light illuminated the sky, flocks of birds cried mournfully, and monks and laity alike wailed in grief, their voices shaking the valleys. After his passing he sat upright for three days, his face fair and his lips red, his hands and feet soft, as though entered into meditative concentration."
From this we can know
that Master Hanshan attained rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss through Buddha-recitation.

Master Hanshan not only recited the Buddha's name himself, seeking rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, but also urged with all his might that all Dharma gates should point toward the Pure Land. In the Dream-Wandering Collection
Preface to The Pure Land as the Point of Return, the Master wrote:

"The one gate of the Pure Land universally covers the three faculties; the sudden and the gradual alike enter it, and no capacity is left unembraced. This is what is called transcending the three realms horizontally,
and it is the most supreme Dharma gate
. Among all the patriarchs from of old, among those who have awakened to mind,
there is not one who did not take this as his final refuge
, such as Nāgārjuna
(Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna)
and Aśvaghoṣa
(Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa)
, who praised it with all their might."
It also says:
Among Chan practitioners of the highest faculties, there is not one who does not take refuge in the Pure Land.
The Annotated Chronicle of Master Hanshan records:
"The Hanshan Ancestor once instructed Fuzheng
(Fuzheng)

saying: 'If in Buddha-recitation one will not bring a mind of firm resolve, but only recites amid fleeting fancies, then the habitual currents secretly streaming within the store consciousness are never seen at all, and so the recitation never shows where a single thought comes to rest.
If Buddha-recitation proves effective, it is even superior to pondering the cypress tree or the dry shit-stick.'
In this gong'an of realizing the truth through Buddha-recitation
(that is, the Chan contemplation of Buddha-recitation)
there is indeed an authoritative source."
